title: Union leaders Sidney Cates and Dave Weinstein; inflexible unions
summary: He remembers the Black local's president Cates and the white local's Weinstein as fine men but inflexible, and thinks the adversarial stance toward record companies was counterproductive.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: Who was that that you had to go out to?
Let's see, what was his name? I think that was Cates.
He was head of the union?

Yeah, he was a fine man. I liked him. He was a fine man, but that didn't help anyone that came. It's just like Dave over at the white local. He was a fine guy, you know, real gentleman, nice to speak with.

Yeah, but they were terribly inflexible about their demands, and they just wouldn't cut you any slack at all. And sometimes their interpretations and methodology were awful, awful tough, just tough. I think counterproductive. I know counterproductive, you know, and I never could convince them. They were convinced even until today. That's the way it is. And it's too bad because what it says is that the union and the record companies are enemies. And I think every union has found out that the company that they're working with no longer can be treated like their enemy, but has to be treated in some kind of cooperative venture spirit if it's going to make sense. There's still a few that don't do it that way, and they have...
